name: Palate expanders (adult)

lead: Palate expanders widen the upper jaw. In adults, miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion (MARPE) or surgically assisted expansion is used for a narrow upper jaw, and looksmaxxers seek it for a wider midface, broader smile and easier breathing.

A screw-driven appliance anchored to the teeth, mini-implants in the palate, or both is turned to separate the midpalatal suture so new bone forms in the gap. Adults often need bone anchorage or surgical help because the suture has matured. Trials report skeletal expansion and some airway changes in selected patients; systematic reviews describe the evidence in late adolescents and adults as limited, and trials rarely measure facial attractiveness.

paras: It is delivered by orthodontists or oral surgeons: an appliance is fitted, adjusted at home over weeks, then held in place while bone fills in, usually followed by braces. Total treatment runs many months.

Reported effects include pain, speech changes, a gap between the front teeth, tongue sores, periodontal changes and variable success in adults. Surgical versions carry operative risks, and the work needs a qualified orthodontist.

angle.text: Adult expansion widens the upper jaw, which can broaden the dental arch, midface and smile. It is an established orthodontic procedure studied for narrow upper jaws and breathing; its effect on overall facial appearance has not been tested.

lead: Palate expanders are orthodontic devices that widen the upper jaw (maxilla) so that upper and lower teeth fit together better. They are most often used in children and adolescents, and adult versions, such as miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion (MARPE) and surgically assisted expansion, are used for transverse maxillary deficiency in patients whose palatal suture has matured [1].

In looksmaxxing communities, adult MARPE is discussed as a way to widen the midface, broaden the smile and improve breathing, and some users seek it for aesthetic reasons. Systematic reviews describe the evidence for MARPE in late adolescents and adults as limited, while trials report skeletal expansion and some airway changes in selected patients [2].

Orthodontists, with oral and maxillofacial surgeons for surgical variants
Moderate for expansion; limited for appearance

paras: Rapid palatal expansion uses a screw turned over days or weeks to widen the arch, followed by months of retention while bone fills the midline gap [1]. Slow expansion uses weekly adjustments [1]. MARPE anchors the appliance to the palate with two to four mini-implants, which allows expansion in some young adults with fused sutures and gives more skeletal and less dental change than tooth-borne devices [1][3]. Surgically assisted expansion (SARPE) involves a surgeon cutting the midpalatal suture before the expander is activated, and is used when the palate has matured [1]. One encyclopedia article states that most adults, and men in particular, may need a surgical assist for consistent results [1].

Palatal expansion was first described in the nineteenth century: Emerson Angell published a report in Dental Cosmos in 1860, and later developers included the Haas expander (reintroduced in the US in 1956) and the Hyrax expander (1968) [1]. Mini-implant-supported designs emerged in the 2010s and are the subject of a growing body of clinical literature [2].

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of MARPE in patients aged 16 and older assessed success rate, skeletal and dental expansion, treatment duration and side effects, and described the evidence on efficacy as limited [2]. An umbrella review of MARPE and a 2023 update on expansion in nongrowing patients compare conventional, surgical and miniscrew-assisted approaches.

A randomized trial of 40 adolescents and young adults compared conventional rapid expansion with MARPE using low-dose CBCT to assess skeletal, alveolar and periodontal effects [3]. A multicenter controlled trial examined MARPE in adults with obstructive sleep apnea and quality of life. Further randomized trials have compared MARPE with tooth-borne expansion during the post-pubertal growth spurt, and compared nasal airflow and skeletal changes after conventional expansion versus MARPE in late adolescents and young adults. The studies' main outcomes are skeletal width, dental effects, airway and pain measures rather than facial attractiveness.

Reported effects of palatal expansion include speech changes and a lisp, extra saliva, pain and headaches when the screw is turned, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth, and changes to bone and periodontal tissues such as bone fenestration and tooth extrusion [1]. The zygomatic buttress limits posterior expansion, so expansion tends to be greater at the front [1]. Older studies cited in the same source found that a third to a half of expansion could be lost before stabilization [1]. Research reports that MARPE can fail to open the suture in some patients, which is why success rate is an outcome in reviews [2].

Looksmax.org has many threads about palate expanders and MARPE, with users asking about age limits, outcomes and the choice between MARPE and jaw surgery. One user planning an expander said it was to help breathing while hoping it would widen the maxilla and improve appearance, and asked others for their aesthetic results. Another encyclopedia article states that sustained tongue pressure is claimed by proponents to widen the upper jaw, that orthotropic practitioners use expanders under professional supervision mainly in children, and that mainstream orthodontic bodies find no credible evidence that mewing reshapes the jaw [4].
